source: Uganda MoH Essential Maternal and Newborn Clinical Care Guidelines / WHO ENCC

entries.text: NEONATAL JAUNDICE: Jaundice is the yellow coloring of a baby's skin and eyes caused by excess bilirubin. NORMAL jaundice: appears after 24 hours of life, mild yellowing of face/chest, baby feeds well and is active. Usually resolves in 1-2 weeks. DANGER jaundice (REFER IMMEDIATELY): (1) Appears within the first 24 hours of life. (2) Yellow colour reaches the palms of hands or soles of feet. (3) Baby is very sleepy, not feeding. (4) Baby has fever or is cold. (5) Dark yellow urine or pale stools. MANAGEMENT: Keep breastfeeding frequently (at least 8 times in 24 hours). Expose baby to indirect sunlight for 30 minutes twice daily (NOT direct harsh sunlight). Monitor for danger signs. If jaundice worsens or baby becomes lethargic → REFER URGENTLY for phototherapy.

NEWBORN BREATHING PROBLEMS: A normal newborn breathes 40-60 times per minute. DANGER SIGNS — REFER IMMEDIATELY: (1) Not breathing at birth (needs immediate resuscitation). (2) Fast breathing: more than 60 breaths per minute. (3) Severe chest indrawing (ribs pulling in with each breath). (4) Grunting sound with each breath. (5) Blue colour (cyanosis) of lips, tongue, or whole body. (6) Nasal flaring. WHAT TO DO: (1) Keep the baby warm (skin-to-skin contact). (2) Keep the airway clear (gently clear mouth/nose if blocked). (3) If not breathing: stimulate by rubbing the back. Begin bag-and-mask resuscitation if trained. (4) REFER URGENTLY to health facility. Do not give anything by mouth if baby has breathing difficulty.

LOW BIRTH WEIGHT / PREMATURE BABY CARE: A baby born before 37 weeks or weighing less than 2.5 kg needs special care. KANGAROO MOTHER CARE (KMC): (1) Place the baby upright between the mother's breasts, skin-to-skin. (2) Cover baby's back with a blanket and wear a wrapper to hold baby in place. (3) Continue KMC 24 hours a day — baby should only be removed for diaper changes and bathing. (4) Breastfeed frequently — at least every 2 hours. If baby cannot suckle, express breast milk and feed with a cup/syringe. (5) Monitor temperature — baby should feel warm to touch. (6) Watch for danger signs: not feeding, fast breathing, fever or cold, convulsions. KMC saves lives. It keeps the baby warm, promotes bonding, and improves breastfeeding. Continue until the baby weighs 2.5 kg and is feeding well.

NEONATAL SEPSIS (NEWBORN INFECTION): Newborn infection (sepsis) can spread rapidly and kill within hours. DANGER SIGNS — REFER IMMEDIATELY: (1) Baby stops feeding or feeds poorly. (2) Very sleepy or difficult to wake. (3) Body temperature: high (>37.5°C) or low (<35.5°C). (4) Fast breathing or chest indrawing. (5) Convulsions. (6) Skin: red, swollen, or has pustules. (7) Umbilical cord: red, swollen, draining pus, or foul-smelling. (8) Abdomen distended (swollen belly). PREVENTION: (1) Clean delivery — hand washing, sterile cord cutting. (2) Apply chlorhexidine to cord stump. (3) Exclusive breastfeeding from first hour. (4) Keep baby warm and clean. (5) Limit handling by many people.

UMBILICAL CORD CARE — CLEAN AND DRY METHOD: Proper cord care prevents neonatal sepsis, a leading cause of newborn death. CORRECT CORD CARE: (1) Apply chlorhexidine 7.1% gel (4% chlorhexidine) to the cord stump once daily for the first 7 days. If chlorhexidine is not available, keep the cord clean and dry. (2) Do NOT apply anything else to the cord — no cow dung, ash, herbs, powder, cooking oil, or saliva. These cause infection. (3) Keep the cord stump exposed to air — fold the nappy below the cord. (4) If the cord gets soiled with urine or stool, clean gently with clean water and dry thoroughly. (5) Do NOT bandage or wrap the cord tightly. (6) The cord stump normally falls off in 7-10 days. (7) Do NOT pull off the cord — let it fall off naturally. DANGER SIGNS — REFER IMMEDIATELY: Redness spreading from the cord to the surrounding skin, pus or discharge from the cord base, foul smell from the cord, swelling around the cord, baby is irritable or feeding poorly, fever or body feels cold. These signs suggest cord infection (omphalitis) which can rapidly progress to sepsis and death.

entries.text: NEONATAL HYPOTHERMIA — KANGAROO MOTHER CARE: Hypothermia (body temperature below 36.5°C) is a major cause of newborn illness and death, especially in premature and low birth weight babies. RISK FACTORS: Born before 37 weeks, birth weight below 2.5 kg, delayed drying after birth, cold environment, bathing too early. SIGNS OF HYPOTHERMIA: Cold to touch (especially feet and abdomen), not feeding well, weak cry, lethargy, slow breathing, skin colour changes (pale, mottled, or bluish). KMC TECHNIQUE FOR WARMING: (1) Undress the baby to only a nappy and cap. (2) Place baby upright on mother's bare chest, between the breasts, skin-to-skin. (3) Turn baby's head to one side to keep the airway clear. (4) Cover baby's back with a blanket. (5) Wrap mother and baby together with a binder or cloth. (6) Continue KMC for as many hours as possible — ideally 24 hours a day. (7) Father or other family member can do KMC when mother needs a break. MONITORING: Check temperature every hour — use a thermometer under the armpit. Normal is 36.5-37.5°C. If temperature does not rise above 36.5°C after 1 hour of KMC, or if it falls below 35.5°C — REFER IMMEDIATELY. Additional warming: warm the room, avoid draughts, warm blankets, do NOT use hot water bottles (burn risk). REFER IF: Temperature stays below 36.5°C despite KMC, baby is lethargic or not feeding, breathing problems, any other danger signs.

entries.text: FEEDING DIFFICULTY IN NEWBORNS: A newborn who cannot feed properly is at risk of hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, dehydration, and death. COMMON CAUSES: Prematurity (weak suck reflex), low birth weight, cleft lip/palate, illness (sepsis, respiratory distress), poor attachment to breast, flat or inverted nipples. ASSESSMENT: (1) Is the baby able to suck at all? (2) How long has the baby not fed? (3) Is the baby alert or lethargic? (4) Are there other danger signs? MANAGEMENT — CUP FEEDING: If the baby cannot breastfeed directly, use cup feeding (not a bottle — bottles cause nipple confusion and are hard to clean). TECHNIQUE: (1) Express breast milk into a clean cup. (2) Hold the baby upright or semi-upright. (3) Rest the cup gently on the baby's lower lip. (4) Tilt the cup so the milk just touches the baby's lip. (5) Let the baby lap the milk — do NOT pour into the mouth. (6) Feed slowly and patiently. HOW TO EXPRESS BREAST MILK: (1) Wash hands. (2) Massage breast gently toward the nipple. (3) Place thumb above and fingers below the areola. (4) Press back toward the chest wall, then compress and release rhythmically. (5) Collect into a clean cup. Express every 2-3 hours to maintain supply. REFER IF: Baby has not fed for more than 3 hours, very weak or no suck reflex, lethargic or difficult to wake, signs of dehydration (dry mouth, sunken fontanelle, fewer wet nappies), any other danger signs.
entries.guideline: Essential Newborn Care / WHO Infant Feeding Guidelines
